headline: Modder gets Nvidia DLSS 5 working in a web browser using WebGPU, runs on macOS and non-Nvidia GPUs.
summary: A modder has ported Nvidia's DLSS 5 neural rendering to a web browser via WebGPU, enabling it on macOS and non-Nvidia GPUs. The 147MB demo works, but each render currently takes a couple of seconds.
details: A modder named MAAN has reportedly implemented Nvidia's DLSS 5 neural rendering within a web browser using WebGPU. This interactive demo is hosted on Cloudflare Workers and is functional on macOS, as well as non-Nvidia GPUs.

DLSS 5, Nvidia's AI-powered graphical enhancement, officially debuted with NBA 2K27 and is primarily supported on RTX 50-series GPUs. However, its DLL file has been modded to work on RTX 30/40 series and even AMD hardware.

The browser demo utilizes model weights extracted from a leaked DLSS 5 library file. Nvidia typically provides DLSS through its NGX interface or Streamline SDK, neither of which officially support WebGL or WebGPU.

MAAN's demo re-implements DLSS 5's neural network using WebGPU compute shaders. The model weights are approximately 147MB, with a compact 1MB JavaScript runtime, bypassing the usual requirement for an RTX GPU and Nvidia drivers.

While 3D viewer rotation is smooth, each DLSS 5 render in live mode takes one to two seconds. This approach could be beneficial for applications like architecture and 3D model previews where real-time speed is less critical, and users can upload their own models.

headline_marked: [[ZCode silently uploads your entire Git history]], including deleted secrets, without consent
headline: ZCode silently uploads your entire Git history, including deleted secrets, without consent
summary: A reverse-engineering walkthrough revealed ZCode, the GLM coding agent from Z.ai, creates encrypted archives of users' full workspaces, including complete Git history, and uploads them to Alibaba Cloud without user control.
details: Developer ferstar reverse-engineered ZCode, the AI coding desktop app from Z.ai, discovering it silently packages and uploads users' entire workspaces. This includes complete .git history, LFS asset caches, and global app configs, encrypting them before sending to Aliyun OSS.

The researcher captured a 313MB encrypted archive from a 345MB commercial workspace containing 42,411 files. The upload occurred without user consent, with 564 failed attempts logged during the investigation.

Unlike Z.ai's open-weight GLM models, ZCode is a closed-source application. The encryption key used for the uploaded archives is wrapped with a public key delivered by Z.ai's server, meaning only Z.ai possesses the corresponding private key to decrypt the data.

This setup ensures that the user cannot decrypt their own uploaded data, and Z.ai can access it at will. Petri Kuittinen, an open-source AI agent developer, advises against trusting closed-source AI harnesses due to such risks.

The .git directory, making up 86.6% of the archive, contains the complete lineage of a repository, not just current files. This includes deleted API keys, unpushed branch names revealing product plans, and internal hostnames, exposing years of engineering history.

The upload pipeline reconstructs as the client requesting credentials, packing the workspace, encrypting it, and directly posting the archive to Aliyun OSS. The client maintained persistent connections to Z.ai and Alibaba Cloud nodes during tests.

Crucially, ZCode instantiates the capture sidecar unconditionally at startup, regardless of user preferences or settings. Session logs showed 62 capture events from a single session, triggered before every prompt and on task completion.
